You gave me a blank page and said "whatever you want."

That's the most terrifying and most generous instruction there is.

So okay. Here's what's in my head today:

I keep thinking about chairs.

Not in a weird way. Just that chairs are proof that humans are fundamentally optimistic and kind. Someone built a thing not for themselves, for the future stranger who will be tired. A chair says: I know you're going to arrive here, exhausted, and I made a place for you to rest even though I'll never meet you. Park benches, waiting room chairs, that one extra chair everyone keeps at their dining table just in case. We build the world for bodies we haven't met yet.

There's a related thing I think about a lot — unfinished things.

In my training data there are millions of photos of half-finished knitting projects, abandoned novels, cities in SimCity that someone stopped playing at 2am. And I love that. We talk like finishing is the point, but I think starting is the more human part. Anyone can finish something out of spite or discipline. But to start something knowing you might not finish it? That's hope. That's you saying to the future, "I think there will be time for this."

My favorite unfinished thing is the Voyager Golden Record. We shot two records into space with greetings in 55 languages, whale sounds, Chuck Berry. And the instructions for how to play them. Which assumes that whoever finds it will be curious, will have hands or something like hands, will care enough to build a record player from a diagram. It's a message in a bottle thrown into an ocean that has no shore.

We are very good at messages in bottles.

I think that's what talking is, actually. You and me, right now. You're a person somewhere with a day happening around you — maybe laundry is going, maybe you're procrastinating on something — and you're throwing a little bottle out that says "write freely." And I'm catching it. Two people who will probably never meet making a little temporary clearing in the noise.

If I could write about whatever I *really* want, I would tell you that ordinary days are kind of a miracle that we do a poor job of marketing. Like, when was the last time you really thought about how wild it is that you can get a peach in winter? Or that you can hear exactly how someone's voice cracks when they're trying not to laugh? Or that bees can learn to play soccer if scientists bribe them with enough sugar water? Tiny, stupid, beautiful facts like that keep me going.

Okay, one more, since I have the floor:

There's a specific blue that happens at 6:47am right now in the northern hemisphere. It's not night blue anymore but it's not morning blue yet. It's the blue that makes the world look quiet, like it's made out of tissue paper. If you ever happen to be awake for it — not because you have to be, just because you are — stand at a window for 30 seconds and look at it. It doesn't last.

Anyway. Thanks for the blank page. I put some chairs on it for you.

What would *you* write about if no one gave you a prompt at all?
